title: On Being a Human
author: John Mark N. Reynolds
summary: John Mark Reynolds reflects on how he first read Homer's Iliad badly, as a boy who wanted to look at Helen rather than honour her as a person, and how a slower graduate-school reading changed that. He argues that Paris and Achilles both reduce a woman to a prize, which harms her and wrecks the Greek army, because a human soul can never be treated as a means to an end. He draws on Dorothy Sayers's question "Are women human?" and on the women of his childhood who simply were women rather than media images. His reading of the epic is that its tragedy is men without women and women without voices, with Achilles divided between a divine mother and a human father and never reaching full humanity. Hector comes closest through his love for Andromache. Reynolds concludes that men are not fully human without women.
points: Reynolds models how the same classic text yields different lessons when it is read hastily as a boy and slowly under a good teacher.
Treating a person as a prize to be won is presented as the common fault of Paris and Achilles, with damage that spreads from the woman to the whole community.
Every human must be an end for every other human, which rules out treating either sex as the add-on or the other.
The Iliad's tragedy is read as the failure of men and women to hear each other, with Achilles unable to become whole because he has no woman's voice in his life.
Hector is the most sympathetic figure because he shows genuine human love for Andromache and sees her as human.
quotes: No human can be a means to an end. Every human must be the end for any other human.

You have taken an eternal thing, a human soul, and used that soul as a means to some selfish end. Achilles fractures the Greek army to get his prize back, and many die, including his friend Patroclus.
No man should treat women as “other,” because the totality of humanity is woman and man.
The thoughtful people in my life, including my mom, said, “Women are human first. Women are their own selves. Women are not ‘the other’ except to you.
At first, the Iliad seems like a “boy book,” but then any human realizes that the tragedy of the Iliad is men without women and women without voices.
Nobody does in the Iliad, though Hector comes closest in the love, genuine human love, he shows to Andromache. She is human to him, and so Hector is the most sympathetic.
Are men human? At the end of the Iliad, the answer is “no, not without women.
